o1.biggest_strength: It acts on the real signals: keep 30%, focus on the top creator-educator partners, fix the credit window and payouts, and keep the plan within the $40,000 perk budget.
o1.biggest_mistake: The $38,000 saving from cutting only new customers is not well supported and likely wrong, and the 90-day credit window is limited to Partners rather than fixing the issue for everyone.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Make the new-customer savings math solid, extend the credit window more cleanly, and tighten the first-30-days finance impacts.

o2.biggest_strength: It gives the clearest money case against the 20% cut, including lifetime value, top-20 concentration, partner defection risk, and the cost of a 90-day window.
o2.biggest_mistake: The 40% first-year Partner tier adds a new commission cost on top of the $40,000 budget when the data says the main complaints are payout speed, minimums, and lost credit, not the rate.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Keep the stronger 90-day-window and cost modelling, but avoid the unnecessary 40% tier unless it is tied to a strict retention or incremental-growth test.

reason: Both are strong, but Output 1 is the plan I would be more comfortable handing to finance and the partner manager tomorrow: it keeps the 30% promise, rewards the top partners without raising headline commission, fixes payouts, and stays inside the stated perk budget. Output 2 has better modelling in places, but the 40% tier spends more before proving the payout and credit fixes are not enough.
